subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Find the derivative of y = cos⁻¹(4x³ − 3x).

mark_split.label: Put x = cos θ and use cos 3θ = 4cos³θ − 3cos θ

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IB (2026-27 edition), book p.194, chapter 9 DIFFERENTIATION, Very Short Answer question 18(i). **Only the question was taken. The answer −3/√(1 − x²) was checked against a numerical difference quotient before it was written: on the stated range both read −3.750000 at x = 0.6, −5.000000 at x = 0.8 and −9.607689 at x = 0.95. A control was also run OUTSIDE that range: at x = 0.2 the difference quotient reads +3.061862, which is +3/√(1 − x²) and not the boxed answer — this is why the range 1/2 ≤ x ≤ 1 is written into the solution rather than left out.

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — name the substitution you make and the identity it turns the bracket into.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Put x = cos θ and use cos 3θ = 4cos³θ − 3cos θ
steps.margin_note: First mark, and the step the rest of the answer depends on. The bracket 4x³ − 3x is the cosine triple-angle expansion written in x. Once x = cos θ is written down, the bracket is cos 3θ and the inverse cosine cancels it.
steps.memory_tip: 4x³ − 3x with a cos⁻¹ outside it always means x = cos θ; 3x − 4x³ with a sin⁻¹ outside it means x = sin θ.
lines: Put x = cos θ, so θ = Cos⁻¹x
Take θ in [0, π/3], that is 1/2 ≤ x ≤ 1. Then 3θ lies in [0, π], the principal range of Cos⁻¹, so

recall.must_convey: That x = cos θ is substituted and 4cos³θ − 3cos θ = cos 3θ, so y = 3 Cos⁻¹x.
accept: put x equal to cos theta and use the triple angle formula
four cos cube theta minus three cos theta is cos three theta
cos inverse of cos three theta is three theta so y is three cos inverse x
x ki cos theta substitute cheste cos three theta vasthundi
the bracket is the cos triple angle expansion

steps.why: Differentiating cos⁻¹(4x³ − 3x) directly by the chain rule gives a long expression with √(1 − (4x³ − 3x)²) in it, which does not simplify by hand inside a 2-mark question. The substitution replaces the whole bracket by a single angle, and the rest is one standard derivative.
common_mistakes: Substituting x = sin θ, which does not match 4x³ − 3x and does not simplify.
Differentiating the bracket directly by the chain rule and being unable to reduce √(1 − (4x³ − 3x)²).
Omitting the range and writing y = 3 Cos⁻¹x for every x, when the sign is different for −1/2 < x < 1/2.

steps.label: Differentiate 3 Cos⁻¹x
steps.margin_note: Second mark. d/dx(Cos⁻¹x) = −1/√(1 − x²). The minus sign belongs to the inverse cosine and must be carried into the boxed line.
steps.memory_tip: Inverse cosine carries a minus and inverse sine does not; everything else about the two derivatives is identical.

recall.must_convey: That d/dx(Cos⁻¹x) = −1/√(1 − x²), so the answer is −3/√(1 − x²).
accept: cos inverse x differentiates to minus one over root one minus x squared
three times that gives minus three over root one minus x squared
the answer is minus three by root one minus x square
cos inverse ki minus vasthundi, so minus three by root one minus x square
keep the minus sign from the inverse cosine

steps.why: Only one standard derivative is left, so this mark is for quoting it with its minus sign. A positive 3/√(1 − x²) is the sin⁻¹ answer to a different question.
common_mistakes: Dropping the minus sign and writing 3/√(1 − x²).
Writing the denominator as 1 − x² without the square root.

insider_note: 4x³ − 3x is cos3θ, so put x = cos θ and the whole thing collapses to 3Cos⁻¹x. Differentiating the original directly is far harder and rarely lands.
